body.text: Wall Street closed its best week in a month on a slightly sour note, as tech stocks were dragged down again over anxieties about Nvidia and AI investments.
The ASX is priced for a flat opening while the Aussie dollar remains under pressure, sliding again to be worst performing G10 currency this month.
Follow the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our live blog.

Miners under pressure as commodity prices slip
Australian miners may come under renewed selling pressure today after another slide in key commodity prices last week.

Copper slipped to its lowest level in almost four months on Friday and was on course for its biggest weekly dip since March while Dalian iron ore futures fell for a third straight session on and logged their biggest weekly loss in five weeks.
Copper shed around 3% last week, its fifth weekly decline in succession and the steepest loss in a week since late March.
Benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange slipped 1.6% to $13,371.50/tonne.

Investment bank Goldman Sachs argues copper's decline has been driven by a selloff in AI-related equities — which copper is exposed to, given its use in electrification and data centres — since the Democratic victory in the US midterms.
Goldman Sachs now sees downside risks to its 2027 copper price forecast of $15,400 a metric ton after the US midterm elections.

However, the bank's commodities team said the correction reflected positioning rather than loosening copper fundamentals, noting that there was limited copper supply in the world's top consumer China, where inventories are low and premiums are high.
Copper stocks in Shanghai Futures Exchange warehouses declined another 18% to just 27,642 tons this week, the lowest since December 2023.
Inventory levels for iron ore at Chinese ports are heading a different direction which, along with softer demand, is putting downward pressure on prices.
Iron ore stocks at 10 major Chinese ports rose 3.3 million tons, or around 3%, week-on-week to 108 million tonnes late last week, data from consultancy Shanghai Metals Market showed.
The most-traded January iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange closed daytime trade 0.5% lower at 669.5 yuan ($US100.39)/tonne.
The contract lost 2.8% last week, its biggest fall since the week ended October 9.
The benchmark December iron ore on the Singapore Exchange was little changed at $US90.40/tonne, losing 2.8% this week.
Over in the gold sector, things are also looking less bright.
Despite a marginal gain on Friday, the spot gold price recorded its biggest weekly fall since March, as traders increased bets of further rate hikes by the Fed.
Elsewhere, in base metal trade on the LME on Friday, aluminium was down 0.6% to $3,011/tonne after earlier hitting $2,982 for its lowest since mid-October.
Zinc dropped 0.3%, while Nickel shed 1.6%.

Nvidia results, Anthropic IPO have Wall Street on edge
Wall Street's third quarter results season has almost wrapped up — bar two of the most significant events in recent times.

Nvidia, the erstwhile "most valuable" company on the planet — around which the fortunes of so many AI players orbit — is spinning a bit off its axis and the market is hoping things will stabilise with a strong result on Tuesday.
On Thursday, trading in Claude chatbot creator Anthropic is expected to begin, setting up a real-time barometer for sentiment on the AI trade.
"The market has rose-coloured glasses on almost all the risks," including inflation and the war in Iran, in addition to uncertainty over AI, Wells Fargo investment boss Sameer Samana.
Mr Samana said disappointments this week "could finally kind of wake investors up from this ability to look at every glass as half full."

The twin worries of Nvidia's position at the heart of the AI's circular and massive investment boom and the departure of its polestar/rock-star CEO Jensen Huang in rather unseemly circumstances has seen the chipmaker's value fall from about $US5.8 trillion in early October to $US3.9 trillion as of Friday.
Analysts expect earnings growth of 90% on revenue of $109 billion in the company's fiscal third quarter. If that's not at least met, then stand clear.
Anthropic's initial public offering is set to value the company at up to $US1.4 trillion, as the AI lab and some of its investors aim to raise up to $US64.4 billion by selling 825 million shares.
Anthropic's Nasdaq listing comes on the heels of the high-profile June IPO for Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $US75 billion at a nearly $1.75 trillion valuation.

Big retailers will also feature this week with Walmart, Target, Home Depot and Lowe's all posting results will give insights into how consumer spending is holding up in the face of mounting inflation.

The local focus this week will be firmly on the labour market with important data on wages (Wednesday) and jobs (Thursday) being released by the ABS.
The Q3 Wage Price Index is expected to show a modest rise as the 4.75% Fair Work Commission increase flows through to pay packets.
The CBA economics team has pencilled in 0.9% quarter-on-quarter rise in the WPI, lifting annual growth to 3.3% from 3.2%.
There was a surprise fall of almost 40-thousand jobs in September, much of which came from changes in design of the ABS survey.
Market economists don't expect a repeat in October with the consensus being just under 30-thousand new jobs being created.
If the participation rate holds steady, the unemployment rate should hold at 4.7%.
There also a bit of action on the RBA front.

Governor Michele Bullock is out and about on Monday, but this time not she is not being grilled by a parliamentary committee nor gently warmed by a "fireside chat" — she'll be chatting with fellow regulators at the ASIC Annual Forum.
The RBA Policy Board minutes come out on Tuesday which will be more interesting than usual given the 6–3 split in the November hike vote.

"We will be watching how the minutes describe the balance of risks (inflation vs economic activity), whether the minority judged policy restrictive enough, and the bar for further hikes," the CBA team says."We see the RBA on hold in December, with the risk of further tightening in 2027if inflation surprises on the upside and economic activity does not slow."

Looking overseas, to be blunt, there's nothing much that's captured the blog's attention — but we are a bit myopic.
Key Event
Aussie dollar's 'tumultuous week'
As mentioned in the earlier post, the AUD/USD is the month's worst-performing G10 currency, off another 0.5% to bring its weekly loss to 1.4% and at 0.6772 its lowest since late January.

NAB's Head of FX Strategy, Ray Attrill described it as a "tumultuous week" for the little Aussie battler, however it has more to do with what's happening on the other side of the Pacific than a flight to safety.
"The year-to-date low, recall, is 0.6663 on 5 Jan," Mr Attrill wrote in a note this morning.
"AUD weakness so far this month is much more of an interest rate story than it is about risk sentiment.

"As well as the collapse in longer duration AU-US spreads, driven more from the US side than Australia, money markets, as well as pricing out almost all of the risk of a December RBA hike (now just 6%), are now more seriously flirting with the possibility of rate cuts next year.
"August 2027 OIS (Overnight Index Swap) pricing, for example, ended Friday at 4.80%, so below the current 4.85% cash rate, down from 4.91% at the end of October."
Key Event
Wall Street slips, ASX going nowhere
Wall Street's week of recovery spluttered to a halt on Friday with the key stock indices mostly closing lower, although the Dow did inch ahead.
• Nasdaq: -0.9%
Despite Friday's retreat, the Nasdaq and S&P 500 both snapped a four-week streak of declines. The S&P 500 gained almost 2.5% over the five sessions.
Eurozone share rose more than 3% over the week, Japan put on 6.5%.
The ASX was a bit muted in comparison, up 0.7%, but it has enjoyed three consecutive weeks of gains.
It looks like being a quiet start to the week, with futures trading pointing to a flat ASX opening.

One of the sharpest movements on Wall Street on Friday was the airline sector — not exactly "adopt brace position", but airline shares dropped in the final minutes of trading after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop of all departing flights.
The NYSE Arca airline index closed down 1.4%.
Nvidia shares also continued to lose altitude, down another 2% on Friday, over uncertainty about leadership at the chipmaker.
It's the sixth consecutive week of losses for the one-time most valuable company on the planet.

CEO Jensen Huang's resignation on Thursday has raised concerns about the durability of the AI trade, given Nvidia's primary role in the industry's boom and its financial ties to a host of companies in the sector, which has been a pillar of the bull market in equities.

"The tech trade, the AI trade, Nvidia is going to go through a period of volatility, and you're going to see the bulls and bears kind of wrestle on where this narrative goes through the rest of the year … there's been a loss of confidence," chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, Anthony Saglimbene told Reuters.

"The market and investors are trying to navigate what does the AI theme look like when we have the absence of Jensen Huang, who was basically the AI champion and willing to use Nvidia's balance sheet to fund a lot of this AI expansion. That's gone."
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 3.4%, with Advanced Micro Devices dropping 8.8% and Broadcom down 4.8% as the biggest drags on the index.
The S&P 500 technology index shed 1.7% and was the worst performing of the 11 major S&P sectors.
But Microsoft ended 0.2% higher, as it erased earlier declines after a global outage that included its Outlook and Teams products began to ease.
On the economic front, slightly softer-than-expected factory gate inflation (PPI) did little to change the view that the Fed would be raising rates next month.
The 2-year US Treasury yield, the bond yield most sensitive to the Fed's rates decisions, registered its largest jump in more than two years.
That sent the US dollar to a two-month high against its major trading partners.

The Aussie dollar was the biggest casualty, down 0.5% to 67.71 cents, making it the worst performing G10 currency this month — partly due to the fact that it is only G10 country for which markets are pricing a rate cut next year.
The Fed rate hike bet is also driving down gold which fell 4.5% last week, though it did manage a marginal gain on Friday.

Oil had a quiet day by its recent standards, although Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 16% and 13% respectively last week as the focus shifts to a global surplus building up and dwindling US demand.
Good morning
Good morning and welcome to another day on the ABC markets and finance blog.
Stephen Letts from ABC business team limbering up for a blow-by-blow coverage of the day's events, where every post is hopefully a winner, but none should be construed as financial advice.
Wall Street closed lower on Friday, once again pulled down by the tech sector.
The ASX appears to be lacking direction with futures trading pointing to a flat opening, or a 2 point drop to be more precise.
The Australian dollar is under pressure, falling 0.5% to under 68 US cents on Friday, as US interest rates push higher.
On the data front, it's quiet locally although we'll get insights in the Chinese economy with the big monthly data drop this afternoon, while Japanese GDP will be worth a look as well.
The game's afoot, so let's get blogging.
